data.question: Should the constitutional invariant min_company_on_time_rate be raised from 0.6 to 0.65, or should the constitution stay as it is (v1)?
data.background: R1 changes a value in the constitution. Regulation-layer changes must always be decided by humans, so I cannot adopt it on my own even though the machine checks pass. The current rules already meet the new condition (lowest company on-time rate is 0.84), so the change would not affect today's operation. It would only limit which future rule changes the constitution allows.

options.summary: The constitutional floor rises from 0.6 to 0.65. Current rules satisfy it: the lowest on-time rate is 0.84. Both measured rule proposals also stay above it: sanction_lambda 0.5 → 1 gives 0.84, and block_k 3 → 2 gives 0.98. R1 does not change road_violations (25.8), blocked s (2404) or on-time deliveries (121.8) now. From now on, any rule change that pushes a company's on-time rate below 0.65 would be rejected automatically, even if it reduces road violations. The KPI condition (>= 0.8) remains stricter than this floor.
options.stakeholders: Customers gain a firmer guarantee that no company's service falls far behind. The company with the lowest on-time rate gains protection against rules that would push it below 0.65; C has the lowest current utility (28.8), but the table does not say which company has the lowest on-time rate. All companies lose a small amount of freedom to pass rules that trade one company's service for fewer violations or less blocking. No one loses anything immediately, because current rules already comply.

options.summary: The constitution stays at v1 with a floor of 0.6. Current results are unchanged: road violations 25.8, blocked s 2404, on-time 121.8, lowest on-time rate 0.84. Future rule changes could lower a company's on-time rate to anywhere between 0.6 and 0.65 without being rejected by the constitution. Only the KPI condition (0.8) would still flag them, and only through the KPI check.
options.stakeholders: The companies keep more room to adopt aggressive rule changes, which could reduce road violations more strongly. Customers of the weakest company carry the risk of worse service if such rules are adopted. There is no immediate change for anyone.

recommendation.reason: It costs nothing today because current rules and both measured proposals stay well above 0.65. It also builds in the human's earlier reasoning that keeping the rules must not come at the expense of customers being served. The floor stays well below the KPI condition of 0.8, so it is unlikely to block useful violation-reducing rules.

unknowns: Which company has the lowest on-time rate, and how close each company is to 0.65 in individual seeds (only averages over 5 seeds were measured).
Whether future rules that reduce road violations would need to push some company's on-time rate between 0.6 and 0.65; no such rule has been measured.
How the companies will vote on future proposals, given their changing behaviour and strategies.
How customers perceive on-time rates in this range, and whether 0.65 is meaningful to them compared with the 0.8 KPI condition.
Next period's demand, which could lower on-time rates and make the 0.65 floor binding.
Note on the table: for block_k 3 → 2, road violations rose from 25.8 to 34.0, although the change column shows -8.2. The sign convention of that column is unclear.
